newsitem.title: USA: Stocks tumble, bonds edge up on stronger dollar.
newsitem.headline: Stocks tumble, bonds edge up on stronger dollar.

text.p: Stock sank Wednesday as investors remained wary after the market's recent sell-off, while bonds edged higher as the dollar strengthened.
Crude oil prices dropped to the lowest level in months as news of growing supplies and the end of the winter heating season fuelled selling by speculators.
The Dow Jones industrial average lost 94.04 points to end at 6,517.01. The Nasdaq Composite index fell 15.93 points to 1,201.00.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,710 to 816 on active volume of 478 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
"Everybody has their horns pulled in," said Arnie Owen, director of equities at Kaufman Brothers.
The blue-chip Dow index was sent reeling Thursday and Monday, posting back-to-back losses that totalled nearly 300 points. That was followed by a 28-point rise on Tuesday.
But investors were not in a buying mood, and Wednesday's downturn put the Dow 8 percent below its record closing high of 7,085.16 set March 11.
The Nasdaq index, which is studded with high-technology stocks, has shed 13.5 percent since its Jan. 22 high of 1,388.06.
The stock market has been sliding since the Federal Reserve raised short-term interest rates last week in an effort to keep the economy from over-heating.

The possibility of additional rate hikes, amid signs the economy was still growing at a steady clip, has led to concerns on Wall Street that rate hikes would cool off the economy and bring a slowdown in corporate profit growth.
A string of economic data showing a resilient economy has fanned fears that last week's hike in short term interest rates would only be the first in a series of increases.
Stocks also were dogged by a jump in the yield for the key 30-year Treasury bond to 7 percent has led many investors to shift to bonds, avoiding the volatile stock market.
In the bond market, the 30-year bond rose 1/32, or 31 cents on a $1,000 bond, and its yield fell to 7.07 percent from Tuesday's close of 7.08 percent.
Analysts said Friday's employment report for March will be critical for the near-term direction in bonds and stocks.
Some traders said the corporate earnings reporting season, which starts next week, could stem the downturn in stocks.
The dollar was boosted by a mixed Japanese economic report and reports suggesting the Fed could raise interest rates again soon.
The dollar rose to 123.24 Japanese yen and 1.6755 German marks from 121.73 yen and 1.6663 marks late Tuesday.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for delivery in May closed at $19.47 a barrel, down 81 cents and its lowest closing price since Aug. 30, 1996.
That price was also the lowest for a spot or first month delivery of crude oil on the exchange since March 4, 1996, when oil closed at $19.20 a barrel.
Pressured by the selling in crude oil, May gasoline closed 2.06 cents lower at 60.61 cents a gallon, and May heating oil down 1.43 cents at 52.52 cents a gallon.
Precious metals prices also slipped, with gold for June delivery at the Commodity Exchange in New York closing down $2.60 an ounce at $352.10.
May silver ended down 13.5 cents at $4.87 an ounce.

Overseas, London's benchmark FTSE 100 share index closed 11.5 points lower at 4,236.6, having fallen as low as 4,219.0. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average climbed 167.71 points or 0.94 percent to 18,037.30.
